turns.speaker: matthew-walker
turns.text: In Why We Sleep, I laid out what short sleep does: the prefrontal cortex loses its grip, and the deep NREM cleanup that clears metabolic waste runs incomplete, so a thin residue of fog accumulates night over night. Daytime focus can't erase that. Fix the input: a fixed wake time including weekends, seven to nine hours, phone out of the bedroom. If fog persists after three weeks, see a doctor about sleep apnea.

tail.position: Engineer fog away first through fixed wake time, seven to nine hours, no bedroom phone
tail.open: whether observing fog helps once sleep is repaired

turns.speaker: cal-newport
turns.text: Matthew Walker says persistent fog is accumulated sleep debt, so fix the input: fixed wake time, seven to nine hours. Sleep matters, but it misses a second source. In Deep Work I described attention residue, from Sophie Leroy's research: each switch leaves part of your mind on the previous task, so a rested person checking messages constantly still works in haze. For one week, protect two ninety-minute blocks daily, phone elsewhere, inbox closed, and rate clarity afterward.

tail.position: Sleep is necessary, but attention residue from constant switching sustains fog; protect unbroken blocks for a week
tail.open: how much of the fog is sleep versus switching

turns.speaker: jon-kabat-zinn
turns.text: Cal Newport says protected ninety-minute blocks will clear the haze that constant switching leaves behind. Try them, as an experiment. But right now, as you read this, notice where the fog sits in your body and what you say to yourself about it. Wanting it erased adds a second layer of strain, like resisting pain, and that layer is the part you can drop today, before any schedule changes.

Jon Kabat-Zinn's strain layer is partly sleep too, since short sleep weakens prefrontal control over the amygdala. So change one lever first: fixed wake time, two weeks, then add blocks.

summary.title: Clear brain fog: stabilize sleep first, then focus or notice
agree: Fixed wake time anchors your brain's clock; keep it seven days a week (all three minds)
Score clarity nightly one to five and note whether you fought the fog (Cal Newport and Jon Kabat-Zinn)
Add two protected ninety-minute focus blocks after ten days of stable sleep (Matthew Walker and Cal Newport)
differ: Matthew Walker and Cal Newport differ on which lever matters most: Matthew emphasizes sleep debt, Cal emphasizes attention residue from constant switching. By turn four they converge—both matter, fix sleep first.
Jon Kabat-Zinn's separate point: the struggle to erase fog is itself suffering. His kindly noticing and Cal/Matthew's behavioral shifts address different layers; both can help.
summary.fits: Matthew Walker anchors the plan in one fixed wake time (turn seven); Cal Newport shifts to agree, calling it the right first lever because it changes only one variable (turn eight). Jon Kabat-Zinn adds the inner shift: feel the fog kindly for three breaths each morning, then each evening score whether you fought it (turn nine). Tell us one thing: when you try this ten-day experiment, which change reaches your clarity first?
summary.next_step: Set one fixed wake time tonight, phone outside bedroom. Tomorrow feel the fog kindly for three breaths. Each evening score clarity one to five.
